lines.en: You're about to buy some bargain bin headphones when you spot a real bargain.
lines.zh: 你正打算买一副放在特价筐里的耳机，这时忽然看到了一款真正划算的。

lines.en: This pair is more expensive, but it's selling for half its usual price.
lines.zh: 这副要贵一些，但它正以平时一半的价格出售。

lines.en: Surely this is the better buy, right?
lines.zh: 那这一款肯定更值得买，对吧？

lines.en: It’s possible!
lines.zh: 有这种可能！

lines.en: However, it’s also possible you’re falling for a psychological trick retailers use to influence what you buy and what you’re willing to pay.
lines.zh: 不过也有可能，你正掉进零售商的一个心理圈套——他们用它来左右你买什么、以及你愿意付多少钱。

lines.en: From the late 1800s, economic theory often assumed that consumers were rational actors who pursued the optimal financial choice.
lines.zh: 从十九世纪末开始，经济学理论通常假定：消费者是理性的行为者，会追求最划算的经济选择。

lines.en: But while consumers are reasonably rational on average, they’re also vulnerable to impulse purchases, savvy salespeople, and other external factors that make them, well, irrational.
lines.zh: 虽说平均而言消费者还算理性，但他们也会受到冲动消费、精明的推销员以及其他外部因素的影响，从而变得——嗯——不那么理性。

lines.en: 20th century psychologists investigating these factors learned that human decision making is rarely perfectly logical.
lines.zh: 二十世纪研究这些因素的心理学家发现：人类的决策过程，很少是完全合乎逻辑的。

lines.en: And by the 1970s, this research informed the birth of behavioral economics, a new field exploring the intersection of economics and psychology.
lines.zh: 到了二十世纪七十年代，这些研究促成了一门新领域的诞生：行为经济学，专门研究经济学与心理学的交叉地带。

lines.en: Behavioral economics operated off a new assumption, introduced by economic sciences laureate Herbert Simon.
lines.zh: 行为经济学建立在一个新的假设之上，这个假设由诺贝尔经济学奖得主赫伯特·西蒙提出。

lines.en: His model, called “bounded rationality,” argued that consumers have limited information, limited time, and various psychological constraints that lead them not to the optimal financial choice, but simply one they feel good about.
lines.zh: 他的模型叫「有限理性」，主张消费者掌握的信息有限、时间有限，还受到各种心理上的制约，这些限制让他们最终作出的，并不是最优的经济选择，而仅仅是一个自己感觉还不错的选择。

lines.en: So how do we decide what's good enough?
lines.zh: 那么，我们是怎么判断「够好了」的呢？

lines.en: Rather than using logic, behavioral economists say we fall back on heuristics— mental shortcuts for making decisions easier and faster.
lines.zh: 行为经济学家认为，我们并不是靠逻辑，而是退回来依靠「启发法」——也就是让决策变得更省事、更快速的心理捷径。

lines.en: For example, the anchoring heuristic suggests that the first piece of information you get becomes your baseline for future decision making.
lines.zh: 举个例子，锚定启发法说的是：你最先得到的那条信息，会成为你日后做决定的基准线。

lines.en: So if a menu's first item costs $50, you'll compare other prices against that reference point.
lines.zh: 所以如果菜单上第一道菜标价 50 美元，你就会拿它当参照点，去衡量其他的价格。

lines.en: Psychologists like Daniel Kahneman thought heuristics predict many consumer choices— which means they can be manipulated to control them.
lines.zh: 丹尼尔·卡尼曼这样的心理学家认为，启发法能预测消费者的许多选择——这也就意味着，它们可以被人操纵，进而左右这些选择。

lines.en: Case in point, while those discounted headphones might be 50% off, it’s also possible the original price was inflated to begin with.
lines.zh: 一个现成的例子：那副打折的耳机虽然是五折出售，但它原来的标价，很可能从一开始就是虚高的。

lines.en: Anchoring is just one of many heuristics retailers exploit.
lines.zh: 锚定效应只是零售商加以利用的众多心理捷径之一。

lines.en: Consider this: which of these cleaning products would you buy?
lines.zh: 想想看：这些清洁用品，你会买哪一款？

lines.en: How about now?
lines.zh: 现在呢？

lines.en: Both are equally effective and basically cost the same, but careful language and pricing makes one more appealing.
lines.zh: 两者的效果其实一样，价格也基本相当，但巧妙的措辞和定价，让其中一个显得更有吸引力。

lines.en: This is the framing effect, and it’s one of several psychological phenomena that short circuit our ability to assign value.
lines.zh: 这就是框架效应，它是好几种会让我们估值能力「短路」的心理现象之一。

lines.en: Here’s an example of another: some American grocery stores tried encouraging customers to bring reusable shopping bags by offering a 5 cent credit.
lines.zh: 再来看另一个现象的例子：美国有些杂货店试图鼓励顾客自带购物袋，办法是给五美分的折扣。

lines.en: But this proved less effective than charging a 5 cent fee for using disposable bags.
lines.zh: 但事实证明，这还不如对使用一次性袋子收取五美分来得更有效。

lines.en: In other words, the desire to avoid losing 5 cents was more motivating than gaining 5 cents.
lines.zh: 换句话说，想避免损失五美分的动力，比得到五美分的动力更大。

lines.en: This is called loss aversion, and retailers trigger this fear of losing value by emphasizing a sale’s scarcity or looming deadline.
lines.zh: 这叫「损失厌恶」。零售商正是通过强调促销所剩无几、或者截止时间迫近，来触发你害怕失去这种优惠的心理。

lines.en: All these tactics suggest our perception of value is more important than what something is actually worth.
lines.zh: 所有这些手段都说明：我们感受到的价值，比东西本身真正值多少钱更重要。

lines.en: And that effect goes deeper than you might think.
lines.zh: 而这种影响的深度，可能超出你的想象。

lines.en: In a 2008 study, subjects were put into MRI machines and treated to samples from five bottles of increasingly expensive wine.
lines.zh: 在二〇〇八年的一项研究中，被试被推进核磁共振成像仪，品尝来自五瓶价格逐级升高的葡萄酒样品。

lines.en: Participants reported preferring the expensive samples, and MRI images confirmed this claim.
lines.zh: 参与者表示自己更喜欢那些贵的样品，而核磁共振的成像也证实了他们所言非虚。

lines.en: But in reality they only tasted three bottles, with the two cheapest pulling double duty as the two priciest.
lines.zh: 但实际上，他们只品尝了三瓶酒——最便宜的那两种被拿来兼职充当了最贵的那两种。

lines.en: Of course, retailers don’t just manipulate your perception, they control the spaces you shop.
lines.zh: 当然，零售商并不只是操纵你的感知，他们还在控制你购物的空间。

lines.en: Supermarkets often place high-margin items at eye level and design stores to guide you past them.
lines.zh: 超市常常把利润高的商品摆在与视线齐平的位置，并且把整个门店设计得会把你从它们面前引过去。

lines.en: Behavioral economist Richard Thaler and legal scholar Cass Sunstein call this subtle product placement “nudge theory,” and it works online as well.
lines.zh: 行为经济学家理查德·塞勒和法学家卡斯·桑斯坦，把这种巧妙的商品摆放叫作「助推理论」，而它在网上同样管用。

lines.en: Sites might nudge you by suggesting related items to purchase or by pre-selecting add-ons.
lines.zh: 网站会通过推荐相关商品，或者预先替你勾选附加项，来悄悄推你一把。

lines.en: So if retailers are boxing you in, what can you do about it?
lines.zh: 那么，如果零售商正在把你团团围住，你能做些什么？

lines.en: First, shop slower.
lines.zh: 第一，慢一点买。

lines.en: Heuristic-based decision making is quick and instinctive, so slowing down to run the numbers can pull back the curtain on a flashy deal.
lines.zh: 基于捷径的决策又快又出于本能，所以放慢脚步、认真算一算账，就能掀开那些花哨交易的幕布。

lines.en: Deciding what a product is worth to you before shopping can help set your own anchors.
lines.zh: 在购物之前先想清楚，这样东西对你而言到底值多少钱，这有助于设定属于你自己的「锚」。

lines.en: And always ask yourself why you want this deal.
lines.zh: 而且要时时问自己：我为什么想要这个划算买卖？

lines.en: Buying something just because it’s a bargain means you might not be in control of your choice.
lines.zh: 仅仅因为便宜就去买，意味着你可能并没有真正掌控自己的选择。

lines.en: Above all, remember that retailers and advertisers aren’t just selling products— they’re designing your choices.
lines.zh: 最重要的是记住一件事：零售商和广告商并不只是在卖产品——他们在设计你的选择。

lines.en: And once you understand the psychology behind their designs, you might gain something even more valuable than a discount: the ability to choose on your own terms.
lines.zh: 而一旦你理解了他们那些设计背后的心理学，你可能就得到了比折扣更加宝贵的东西：按照自己的心意做选择的能力。
